chunks: Why ground probe points matter. The question: Why are ground probe points important?
A ground probe point is a small ground pad placed right next to a test point, so an oscilloscope probe can touch both with a very short ground connection.
It matters because the probe's ground lead becomes part of the circuit you are measuring.
A long lead acts as an inductor, and together with the probe tip's capacitance it rings on fast edges. You then see ringing on the screen that is not really on the board.
Imagine measuring the water pressure in a pipe through a long, floppy hose.
Every time the pressure jumps, the hose wobbles, and your gauge shows the wobble as well as the pressure. A short, stiff connector gives a true reading.
A long ground clip is the floppy hose, and a spring tip on a nearby ground pad is the short connector.
The analogy is loose: the "wobble" is an electrical resonance between the lead's inductance and the tip's capacitance.
The step source charges the probe tip capacitance through R s , and the charging current returns through the ground-lead inductance.
That's a series RLC whose output across C p is what the scope displays; if L g is large the response overshoots and rings.
Oscilloscope: an instrument that draws voltage against time on a screen. Ground lead inductance: about 1 nanohenries for each millimeter of lead.
Inductance resists sudden changes in current. Probe tip capacitance: the roughly 10 picofarads a standard probe adds at its tip.
Ringing: a decaying wobble after a fast edge, as energy sloshes between inductance and capacitance.
Resonant frequency: the rate of that wobble, f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) .
Use the probe tip's 10 picofarads.
A 150 mm alligator-clip ground lead is about 150 nanohenries, so f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of 150 nanohenries times 10 picofarads ) is about 130 megahertz.
A 1 nanoseconds edge contains frequencies up to about 350 megahertz, so it sets off that ring.
A spring ground of about 15 mm is 15 nanohenries, which gives about 411 megahertz, and the overshoot falls from about 52% to about 7%.
The board did not change, only the ground path. That is the whole idea.
"The probe's ground lead is a real inductor, about 1 nanohenries per millimetre, and with the probe's roughly 10 picofarads tip capacitance it forms an LC circuit.
A 150 mm clip lead resonates near 130 megahertz and shows about 50% overshoot on a fast edge that isn't really there; it also picks up magnetic fields through its loop.
A ground pad right next to the test point, with a spring ground, brings the resonance up to hundreds of MHz and cleans up ripple and edge measurements.
Ground points also serve production test and debug."
